verdicts.trueWording: are shared among them: entropy reduction, order preservation, and slope preservation
verdicts.note: Abstract of arXiv:2009.07243v1 (PDF -> pdftotext -layout), fetched live from arxiv.org. The three algorithms named earlier in the same abstract are top-k, nucleus and tempered sampling; Section 5.1 restates the same three core properties as shared among those sampling algorithms.

verdicts.trueWording: violating the identified properties could lead to drastic performance degradation
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that violating ANY ONE of the three properties produced the large drop: Section 5.2 finds random mask sampling, which violates order preservation, on par with the existing algorithms, and concludes order preservation could be further relaxed; the degradation is attributed only to violating entropy reduction or slope preservation, and the abstract hedges with 'could lead to'.
verdicts.note: Quotation is verbatim in the abstract, and the second half of the claim (new algorithms satisfying all three perform on par with the existing ones) is supported there and in Section 5.3. Only the unqualified 'violating one of the three properties' limb overreaches.

verdicts.trueWording: primarily optimized for fooling humans. This comes at the expense of
verdicts.note: Abstract of arXiv:1911.00650v2, live PDF. The abstract continues that this introduces statistical abnormalities making detection easy for automatic systems, covering the second limb; the three strategies benchmarked are top-k, nucleus and untruncated random sampling.

verdicts.trueWording: up to 80% of its mass in the first 500 most
verdicts.note: Found in the 'Why are top-k's samples so easy to detect?' paragraph of the Automatic Detection Results section (numbered 7 in this v2 PDF, not 4 as the page field says). The 1,100-token-type limb is verbatim in the next sentence for the other sampling methods and human text. Scope note: the Figure 2b caption states the measurement is of the FIRST token generated in each sequence; the body sentence the claim paraphrases carries no such qualifier.

In the 'Human Evaluation' paragraph of the Automatic Detection Results section (Figure 3b), which reads that even with multi-paragraph 192-length excerpts performance is only 71.4%; it is overall human performance across all sampling methods, pooling the AMT and expert rater pools. Section number in the page field (4) is off; the content matches.

verdicts.trueWording: even multi-sentence excerpts can fool expert human raters over 30%
verdicts.note: Final clause of the abstract of arXiv:1911.00650v2, preceded by the statement that both human and automatic detector performance improve with longer excerpt length. Claim's 'still fooled' renders the paper's 'can fool'.

verdicts.trueWording: temperature is weakly correlated with novelty
verdicts.note: Abstract of arXiv:2405.00492v1, live PDF. The positive direction is stated in the second Introduction bullet, which reports a weak positive correlation between temperature and novelty alongside a negative one for coherence; the task is narrative generation with a fixed context, model and prompt.

verdicts.trueWording: far more nuanced and weak than suggested by the creativity parameter
verdicts.note: Abstract of arXiv:2405.00492v1, with the same sentence repeated at the end of the Introduction. The abstract attributes this to the 'creativity parameter' claim, matching the claim's 'the label creativity parameter implies'.

verdicts.trueWording: for this specific prompt and model, is unable to produce more diversity
verdicts.note: Results paragraph of arXiv:2405.00492v1. The semantic limb is stated a few lines later: outputs at higher temperatures do not extend much further away from the exemplar story than outputs at lower temperatures (cosine similarity, Figure 1b). The exemplar is defined in the Introduction as the greedy sample for that context. The paper's hedge is 'not much further'; the claim drops 'much', though the same paragraph's opening sentence is unqualified.

verdicts.trueWording: higher temperatures (t > 1.0) do not necessarily lead to more diversity
verdicts.note: Results paragraph of arXiv:2405.00492v1. The immediately preceding clause grounds it in the normalised edit distance measure of Figure 1c relative to the exemplar story, and notes an immediate diversity effect already at lower temperatures (.334 < t < 1.0).

verdicts.trueWording: aligns with natural language more closely than text produced using other
verdicts.note: Section 5.5 'Consistent Trends' of arXiv:2106.00085v3, of text generated under the nucleus sampling decoding scheme versus other generation strategies. Corpus limb confirmed under 'Natural Language Corpus': English Wikipedia Dumps. Two hedges the claim drops: the paper says 'often' aligns more closely, and Section 5.4 records that LSTM text under random sampling follows all three of the length, stopword and symbol distributions the closest of any model.

verdicts.trueWording: beam sampling leads to strong divergence from natural language distributions
verdicts.note: Section 5.4 'Length, Stopwords and Symbols' of arXiv:2106.00085v3, with 'across the board' following, and Table 3 holding the empirical-cdf comparisons for exactly those three distributions. Corpus is English Wikipedia Dumps.

verdicts.trueWording: we take this as quantitative evidence for recent qualitative observations
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the rank-frequency results: the 'this' taken as quantitative evidence for repetitive babbling is only the type-token finding of Section 5.2, namely the two transformer models' visible fall-off in unique words for longer-length sequences, described there as a deficiency seemingly specific to the transformer architecture. No rank-frequency result is cited for the babbling observation.
verdicts.note: The quoted fragment 'tend to babble repetitively' is verbatim in Section 5.2, attributed to Holtzman et al. 2020, Cohen and Beck 2019, and Eikema and Aziz 2020, with 'when left to generate lots of text' matching the claim's 'left to generate at length'.

verdicts.trueWording: the limitation of using adherence to Zipf's law as a gauge
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the stated reason. Section 5.1 grounds the Zipf conclusion in a rank-frequency comparison alone: models fit a Zipfian distribution no more poorly than natural language does, the qualitatively worst text (a trigram model under beam sampling) follows the power law most closely, and models nonetheless learn empirical rank-frequency trends well. Type-token divergence is not offered as the reason; Section 5.2, from which the supplied quotation comes, reports transformers under nucleus sampling matching the type-token trend most closely.
verdicts.note: Supplied quotation is verbatim but sits in Section 5.2, one section after the conclusion the claim reports. The paper does contrast the two elsewhere in 5.2 (type-token more disparate from the empirical natural language distribution than rank-frequency), but never as the basis for the Zipf ruling.

verdicts.trueWording: that inadvertently include more noise tokens at higher temperatures
verdicts.note: Abstract of arXiv:2411.07641v1, live PDF. Top-p and min-p are the two methods named in that sentence, and the same sentence states top-nSigma maintains a stable sampling space regardless of temperature scaling; the abstract's second sentence establishes the logit-space statistical threshold.
